profiles.name: Leon Belasco
profiles.excerpt: Leon Belasco combined serious musical training with a long acting career, bringing both talents to radio as Pegon Zellschmidt on A Man Called X.
profiles.bio_html:
Leon Belasco was born Leonid Berladsky in Odessa in 1902 and spent part of his youth in Japan and Manchuria. He trained as a violinist and became concertmaster of the Japanese-Russian Symphony Orchestra before settling in California, where film, stage and radio gradually displaced music as his principal public career.

Radio gave Belasco one of his most enduring roles as Pegon Zellschmidt on A Man Called X. Opposite Herbert Marshall as intelligence agent Ken Thurston, Belasco played the resourceful, comic informant whose implausible relatives and international connections repeatedly placed him in the middle of espionage plots. His musical background remained more than biographical decoration: violin performance and musicianship were genuine professional skills alongside acting.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 65 A Man Called X performances credited to Belasco. That concentrated holding documents the role that most clearly joins his cosmopolitan screen persona, comic timing and radio craft.

profiles.name: Theodore von Eltz
profiles.excerpt: Theodore von Eltz carried decades of stage and film experience into radio, becoming a polished character player across anthology, suspense and family drama.
profiles.bio_html:
Theodore von Eltz was born in New Haven, Connecticut in 1893, the son of a Yale professor. He began acting on the New York stage in the 1910s and became a leading man in silent films before the arrival of sound shifted him toward character parts. By the time radio drama reached maturity, he had already spent decades learning how to define a role quickly and economically.

Von Eltz adapted naturally to microphone work. He played Henry Barbour on One Man's Family in the late 1940s and appeared widely in dramatic anthologies and suspense programs. Radio used the same qualities that sustained his screen career: a controlled, cultivated delivery that could suggest authority, menace or social polish without visual help.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 11 NBC University Theater performances credited to von Eltz, six The Whistler appearances, five each on A Man Called X and This Is Your FBI, four The Adventures of Philip Marlowe episodes and additional work on Escape, Lux Radio Theatre and Screen Directors Playhouse.

profiles.name: Jess Kirkpatrick
profiles.excerpt: Jess Kirkpatrick moved from football and jazz into a decade of Chicago announcing before becoming a prolific Hollywood radio and screen character actor.
profiles.bio_html:
Jess Kirkpatrick was born in Illinois in 1897 and attended the University of Illinois, where he played football and also supported himself as a drummer. Music and broadcasting led him into radio, and he spent roughly a decade as an announcer at Chicago station WGN before moving west.

Kirkpatrick's announcing background became a second professional foundation for his later acting career. In Hollywood he worked in films and television while continuing to appear across radio comedy, westerns and drama. His microphone experience made him especially useful as a supporting player who could deliver authority, comedy or plainspoken realism without calling attention away from the lead.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 19 Wild Bill Hickok performances credited to Kirkpatrick, ten Fibber McGee and Molly appearances, six Gunsmoke episodes, five each on The Great Gildersleeve and The Whistler, four each on Have Gun, Will Travel and Roy Rogers, and three The Railroad Hour broadcasts.

profiles.name: Whitfield Connor
profiles.excerpt: Whitfield Connor began in radio before building an acclaimed stage career and later working as a director and producer as well as an actor.
profiles.bio_html:
Whitfield Connor was born in Ireland in 1916 and entered radio in the 1930s. He reached Broadway in the 1940s and won a Theatre World Award for his work as Macduff opposite Michael Redgrave in Macbeth, establishing a stage career that ran alongside film, television and broadcasting.

Connor later expanded beyond performance into directing and producing, making those roles a genuine second branch of his professional identity. His radio work shows the earlier foundation: he appeared across police drama, literary anthology and contemporary suspense, bringing stage-trained clarity to parts that could range from officials and investigators to ordinary men under pressure.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 15 This Is Your FBI performances credited to Connor, 13 NBC University Theater broadcasts, ten Dragnet appearances, nine Tales of the Texas Rangers episodes, seven Broadway Is My Beat performances and additional work on Escape, Crime Classics and Screen Directors Playhouse.

profiles.name: Rhoda Williams
profiles.excerpt: Rhoda Williams grew up at the microphone and became the original radio Betty Anderson on Father Knows Best while also building a durable voice-acting career.
profiles.bio_html:
Rhoda Williams was born in Denver in 1930 and began performing in radio as a child. She proved capable of handling professional schedules at a young age and developed into one of the juvenile performers who could work alongside adult repertory casts without being treated merely as novelty talent.

Her defining radio role was Betty Anderson, the oldest daughter on the NBC version of Father Knows Best, opposite Robert Young. Williams also worked in film and voice acting, including Drizella in Walt Disney's Cinderella, and later supplied voices for other screen and themed-entertainment productions. Her career demonstrates the continuity between radio acting and the developing American voiceover profession.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 53 Father Knows Best performances credited to Williams, four Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts, two Dr. Christian appearances and additional work on Have Gun, Will Travel and Sears Radio Theater.

profiles.name: Teri Keane
profiles.excerpt: Teri Keane was a durable New York radio actress whose career stretched from daytime serials into the 1970s revival of network drama.
profiles.bio_html:
Teri Keane was born in Manhattan in 1925 and grew up in a household closely connected to journalism and music. Radio became her principal early medium, and she built the kind of schedule associated with New York professionals who moved among daytime serials, anthology drama and live network productions.

Keane appeared on programs including The Road of Life, The Romance of Helen Trent, The Second Mrs. Burton and Just Plain Bill. She later spent twelve years on television's The Edge of Night, but returned to radio drama through CBS Radio Mystery Theater, where her experience made her part of the repertory that sustained the network revival.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 40 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances credited to Keane, eight X Minus One episodes, five each on Theater Five and Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, two Barrie Craig appearances and an additional Gang Busters performance.

profiles.name: Jean Tatum
profiles.excerpt: Jean Tatum was a busy West Coast radio actress whose strongest surviving GRH record is in Johnny Dollar, supported by suspense, detective and police drama.
profiles.bio_html:
Jean Tatum belongs to the large group of professional radio performers for whom the surviving broadcast record is far fuller than the surviving personal biography. Cast logs place her repeatedly in West Coast dramatic production during the 1940s and 1950s, especially in crime and suspense programs that depended on experienced repertory actors.

Tatum's credits show the range expected of that system. She appeared frequently on Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar and also worked on The Whistler, A Man Called X, Dragnet, Broadway Is My Beat and other dramatic series. Rather than being defined by one continuing character, her radio career was built around moving convincingly from one story and role to the next.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 40 Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances credited to Tatum, five The Whistler appearances, three A Man Called X episodes, two Dragnet performances and additional work on Broadway Is My Beat, Let George Do It, NBC University Theater and Richard Diamond, Private Detective.

profiles.name: Richard Denning
profiles.excerpt: Richard Denning was already an established film actor when radio gave him one of his most important comedy roles as Lucille Ball's husband on My Favorite Husband.
profiles.bio_html:
Richard Denning was born Louis Albert Heindrich Denninger Jr. in New York in 1914 and grew up in Los Angeles. After studying business and working in his father's garment company, he entered acting through a radio contest that led to a screen test and a Paramount contract. World War II interrupted his film career when he served in the United States Navy.

Denning returned to broadcasting after the war and became George Cooper opposite Lucille Ball's Liz on My Favorite Husband. The CBS situation comedy developed the domestic format and writing team that would help lead to I Love Lucy. Denning's straight-man performance was central to making Ball's comic schemes work, and radio remained one of the most substantial starring assignments of his career.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 60 My Favorite Husband performances credited to Denning. That concentrated collection captures his best-known radio role and an important bridge between network radio comedy and the television sitcom that followed it.

profiles.name: Guy Sorel
profiles.excerpt: Guy Sorel became a dependable New York repertory actor across the 1960s and 1970s radio-drama revivals, especially Theater Five and CBS Radio Mystery Theater.
profiles.bio_html:
Guy Sorel was born in Paris in 1914 and built an American acting career across stage, film, television and radio. His screen work was largely supporting, but radio offered the kind of repertory environment in which a versatile character actor could return week after week in entirely different roles.

Sorel became part of the regular company of ABC's Theater Five in the mid-1960s and later worked extensively on CBS Radio Mystery Theater. Those two series belong to separate efforts to restore serious network radio drama after the medium's commercial peak, and Sorel's presence in both gives his career an important place in that continuation of the repertory tradition.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 35 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances credited to Sorel, 21 Theater Five appearances, two X Minus One episodes and an additional Cloak and Dagger performance.

profiles.name: Jack Benny
profiles.excerpt: Jack Benny transformed a real violinist's training into one of radio comedy's greatest character jokes, building a program whose timing and ensemble style influenced generations of broadcasting.
profiles.bio_html:
Jack Benny was born Benjamin Kubelsky in Chicago in 1894 and grew up in Waukegan, Illinois. He trained seriously on the violin and entered vaudeville as a musician before discovering that his pauses, reactions and self-deprecating jokes drew stronger laughter than the music itself. By the early 1930s he had reshaped that stage act for radio.

The Jack Benny Program became one of network radio's defining comedies. Benny played a fictional version of himself who was vain, stingy, perpetually 39 and hilariously bad at the violin, even though the real performer was an accomplished musician. The show's ensemble, including Mary Livingstone, Eddie Anderson, Don Wilson, Dennis Day, Phil Harris and Mel Blanc, turned character relationships and timing into a durable situation-comedy form that moved successfully into television.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 50 The Jack Benny Program performances credited to Benny, two each on Lux Radio Theatre, The Fred Allen Show and The Phil Harris-Alice Faye Show, and additional appearances on Lum and Abner and The Halls of Ivy. His violin training is retained as a genuine second professional facet because music was the foundation from which his comic persona grew.
